idiom_name: Channel<T>(capacity = N) with suspend send/receive, close, produce/consumeEach
implementation_notes: The kotlinx.coroutines Channel is the documented replacement for a BlockingQueue: send suspends instead of blocking the thread, receive suspends instead of blocking, the produce {} builder wraps a producer coroutine whose channel closes when the block completes, and consumeEach (or an explicit for loop over the channel) is the consumer side; kotlinlang.org states the analogy to BlockingQueue directly. Capacity is explicit - Channel(capacity = 64) or the RENDEZVOUS, BUFFERED, CONFLATED and UNLIMITED constants - and a closed channel ends receive loops, which is the shutdown protocol; everything participates in structured concurrency, so cancelling the scope cancels producers and consumers together. On the JVM, java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue remains available for thread interop, but inside coroutines a Channel is the idiom.
pitfalls: consumeEach cancels the channel when it completes, so it cannot be shared by several consumers; use an explicit for loop for fan-out (called out in the kotlinlang channels documentation).
Channel(UNLIMITED) and the default buffered capacity remove the bound, so the producer can no longer be backpressured.
A cancelled parent scope cancels the producer, closing the channel early; handle cancellation explicitly if the pipeline must outlive the scope.
send on a closed channel throws ClosedSendChannelException - closing must be single, deliberate and owned.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue for thread interop
variants.implementation_notes: When the producers or consumers are platform threads - interop with Java libraries, ExecutorService pools, or code that must not depend on kotlinx.coroutines - Kotlin uses the Java queue directly: put/take block the calling thread, offer/poll with a timeout bound the wait, and the shutdown protocol is the Java poison pill. This trades the coroutine advantages (suspension instead of blocking, structured concurrency, cooperative cancellation) for zero dependencies and direct interoperability; a coroutine blocked in take() occupies its dispatcher thread, so pool sizing becomes the capacity constraint again.
variants.code_sketch:
val queue = ArrayBlockingQueue<Job>(1024)
val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)
repeat(4) { pool.execute { while (true) handle(queue.take()) } }
queue.put(job)   // producer, any thread
pitfalls: take() blocks a dispatcher thread when called from a coroutine; wrap it in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or use a Channel instead.
InterruptedException must be handled (or the interrupt flag restored) and the consumer loop written to exit cleanly on shutdown.
LinkedBlockingQueue's default is unbounded - the same trap as in Java.
